spans.content: Genetic Detection of Hantaviruses in
Rodents, Albania
Anna Papa,1 * Elton Rogozi,2 Enkelejda Velo,2 Evangelia Papadimitriou,1 and Silvia Bino2
1 Department of Microbiology, School of Medicine, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Thessaloniki, Greece
2 Department of Epidemiology and Infectious Diseases Control, Institute of Public Health, Tirana, Albania
In order to have a first insight into the
epidemiology of hantaviruses in Albania, 263
small mammals (248 rodents, 15 insectivores)
were captured in 352 locations in 29 districts
and tested for hantavirus infection. Dobrava–
Belgrade virus (DOBV) was detected in 10 of
Apodemus flavicollis rodents.
DOBV-positive A. flavicollis were detected in
six districts (Diber, Korce, Kolonje, Librazhd,
Pogradec, and Vlore). The obtained nucleotide
sequences were highly similar to each other
and to DOBV sequences from northwestern
Greece. Understanding the epidemiology of
hantaviruses and identifying the endemic foci
enables the public health strategies to mini-
mize the risk of human infection. J. Med.
2016 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.
KEY WORDS: hantavirus; rodents; Albania
INTRODUCTION
Hantaviruses
(genus
Hantavirus,
Family
Bunyaviridae) are transmitted to humans via inhala-
tion of aerosolized excreta of infected rodents, and
cause to humans hemorrhagic fever with renal syn-
drome (HFRS) in Eurasia, and hantavirus pulmonary
syndrome (HPS) in the US. Like other members of
the Bunyaviridae family, hantaviruses have a tri-
segmented negative-sense RNA genome composed of
the small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments.
The main hantaviruses which cause human disease
in Europe are Dobrava–Belgrade virus (DOBV) asso-
ciated with Apodemus flavicollis, Apodemus agrarius,
and Apodemus ponticus, and Puumala virus (PUUV)
associated with Myodes glareolus. DOBV strains
associated with A. flavicollis and A. ponticus have the
potential to cause the most severe form of HFRS,
which is characterized by fever, headache, gastroin-
testinal symptoms, renal dysfunction, and hemor-
rhagic manifestations, with a fatality rate of
approximately
[Papa, 2012; Kruger et al., 2015].
HFRS is endemic in the Balkan Peninsula and
sporadic cases or outbreaks are observed every year.
Groups at increased occupational risk for infection are
farmers, shepherds, forest workers, and soldiers. The
main hantavirus in southern Balkan countries is
DOBV, while PUUV infections predominate in north-
ern Balkans. For example, DOBV was detected in all
PCR-positive HFRS cases in Greece, while approxi-
mately
of HFRS cases in Slovenia and Croatia are
caused by PUUV [Papa et al., 1998; Avsic Zupanc
et al., 2014]. The Republic of Albania is a Balkan
country consisting of 36 districts. The country is
mostly hilly and mountainous. Since 1985 when the
first HFRS case was serologically confirmed in Albania
[Eltari et al., 1987], only few reports exist [Puca et al.,
2011, 2012]. In a study conducted during 2003–2006
among 34 Albanian patients with suspected Crimean
Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF), CCHF virus was
detected in 13 cases, while four patients were serologi-
cally diagnosed as hantavirus infections [Papa et al.,
2008]. In order to provide a first insight into the
epidemiology of hantaviruses in Albania, small mam-
mals trapped in several regions of Albania were tested
for probable hantavirus infection.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Animals and Samples
A total number of 263 small mammals were
captured using snap traps during 2006–2007 in field
surveys conducted in 352 locations in 29 districts of
Albania (Supplementary Table SI). Among them, 96

tion using previously described RT-nested PCR proto-

hantaviruses associated with rodents of the Murinae
and Arvicolinae subfamilies, respectively [Papa et al.,
1998]. A different RT-nested PCR was applied for
insectivores (Crocidura spp. and Talpa spp.) [Arai
et al., 2007]. PCR products were sequenced and the
nucleotide sequences were aligned by using
Clustal W; a phylogenetic tree was constructed
applying the neighbor-joining method by using
MEGA v6 [Tamura et al., 2013].

DOBV-positive A. flavicollis rodents were detected
in six districts of Albania (three in Diber, three in
Korce, and one each in Kolonje, Librazhd, Pogradec,
and Vlore) (Fig. 1). Characteristics related with the
DOBV-positive animals and the trapping sites are
seen in Supplementary Table SII. It can be seen that
all sites were in shrubbery or forested areas, nearby
canals, streams, or ponds, with a mean altitude of
866 meters above sea level (range 266–1494 meters).
Phylogenetic analysis showed that all sequences
were clustered together with DOBV sequences
obtained from rodents or HFRS patients from other
Balkan countries (Fig. 2). Nucleotide sequences were
submitted to the GenBank database and assigned
accession numbers KT971005 through KT971014.

DISCUSSION
Given that hantaviruses are a frequent cause of
human disease in the Balkan peninsula, it is essen-
tial to identify their endemic foci in the countries in
order to facilitate the public health interventions.
The present study provides a first insight into the
epidemiology of hantaviruses in Albania extending
the knowledge about their distribution in the Bal-
kans. It was shown that all positive samples came
only from A. flavicollis and that
of this rodent
species were infected by DOBV. The respective
percentage in the neighboring Greece is
, where
endemic foci are present in the mountainous areas of
northwestern and northeastern part of the country
[Papa et al., 2000a; Papa and Antoniadis, 2001]. A
previous study showed that A. flavicollis is the most
common and widespread small mammal in Albania,
except for coastal lowlands where Apodemus
sylvaticus predominates. The typical habitats pre-
ferred by A. flavicollis are non-inhabited forested and
shrub areas with altitude ranging from 150 to
1 3 5 0 \mathrm { m }
[Rogozi et al., 2013].
The DOBV prevalence was significantly higher in
male
than in female A. flavicollis
Higher DOBV prevalence among male A. flavicollis,
especially those having scars, has been previously
reported, supporting the hypothesis that hantavi-
ruses are transmitted when aggressive male animals
fight [Papa et al., 2000a].
DOBV-positive A. flavicollis rodents were detected
in six districts of Albania (Diber, Korce, Kolonje,
Librazhd, Pogradec, and Vlore). In general, the
distribution of hantaviruses is closely related with
the population of the rodent reservoirs. Indeed,
Korce, Kolonje, and Librazhd are the districts with
the highest A. flavicollis density [Rogozi et al., 2013].
Although hantaviruses have been detected in several
rodent and insectivore species, DOBV was the only
hantavirus detected in Albania, and A. flavicollis was
the only rodent species found DOBV-positive. Simi-
larly in Greece, the majority of HFRS cases are
caused by DOBV, with very few cases caused by
PUUV [Papa et al., 1998, 2000b; Papa and Antonia-
In conclusion, the present study showed that
DOBV is present in Albania, as in other Balkan
countries. Therefore, surveillance studies and aware-
ness of the physicians are needed, especially in the
regions where DOBV-positive rodents have been
identified. Since it is not unexpected that additional
rodent and/or insectivore species are infected with
hantaviruses, further studies in small mammals are
needed to increase our knowledge on the genetic
diversity of hantavirus strains in Albania, while
seroepidemiological and molecular studies in HFRS
patients will show the spatial and temporal distribu-
tion of cases and the risk for the disease.
